She peered at Misa for a moment longer.

I know I'm speaking in riddles. The truth is I've been given the same riddles. I've been given the conclusions without the premises. That's how it is. But I mean what I say about the risks. We have been forced to keep everything out of the light.

She turned her head slightly, so that Misa could see the red ribbon hidden behind her hair, twin to the one in the Cult headquarters. She held that pose just long enough for Misa to take the meaning.

I do wish She'd be more open with me, though I suspect I know why She won't be. But, even so, I must continue to fight this battle. You don't need to. Frankly, I hate recruiting people into it, and we already have more than I'd like.

Homura closed her eyes for a moment.

I know that's a lot to take in. Under better circumstances, I'd appeal to your faith in the Goddess to let us walk away, but I have to ask for more than that. I have to ask for so much you'll certainly balk; I would in your place. So I'll have to offer you something else.

---

The next memory was tagged differently, and Kyouko realized with a start that it didn't have Misa Virani's metadata. Instead, the files were labeled as if they came from Akemi Homura.

"Homura gave you memories?" Kyouko asked, dumbfounded.

Van Rossum raised an eyebrow, suddenly miffed that Kyouko had gotten the memories first. Or jealous, Kyouko thought.

"Then I blew up the facility myself to hide her tracks, and let them Reformat me to wipe it all away, even the feelings regarding Hermina's 'death' that led me there. So her memories were obviously pretty convincing."

She paused for a moment to make sure she had their attention.

"I've reordered them to be chronological," Misa commented. "So they'd form a cohesive narrative. Most of these I actually got later, either as part of a new recruit package or just recently. Homura believes in making sure we have all the necessary context, in a hard‐to‐fake way. I can't provide you the magic certs, so you'll have to take my word here, but they're real. May the Goddess strike me down where I stand if I'm lying."

"Since when do you believe in the Goddess?" Gracia asked. "No, wait, that's obvious."

The man that was Misa's current body shook his head, laughing to himself.

"You remember when I gave Mina a good zap, right after she made a vow like that? On Karnāta? Nevermind—Kyouko, you know Homura. You'll recognize that these memories are real. Just experience them."

---

The first tranche of memories dated as early as 2440, covering the only period where Internal Security's tracking efforts had met with any success. Even then, this was much more informative, of course—Kuroi Nana would have a keen professional interest in these memories, for the sake of validating the effectiveness of her methods if nothing else.

Homura had wandered the battlefields of the early war, across the Ganges Sector, infiltrating alien positions, monitoring activity and taking notes, and at times intervening from the edges of battles, a silent contributor to some early war defensive stands. Occasionally, she retreated to Optatum for supplies, but she met with no one, evading friendly and enemy patrol alike with stealth magic Kyouko had never seen. And when had she gotten a chance to squirrel away a personal ship?

Still, it was no more than what might be expected of the most capable magical girl who ever lived, turned loose.

Of more interest to Kyouko, these memories heavily censored Homura's emotional state, focusing only on the details of her actions. Might that censorship be aimed, not only at some external audience, but against Homura herself? Was this how she had gotten herself back under control? She had clearly worked hard to hollow out these memories.

No, Kyouko concluded. Homura had never rejected suffering. She just didn't want to share it with others.

Even so, glimmers of a dark, fatalistic mood flickered through. It was more ineffable sentiment than concrete notion: the hesitation before healing an injured arm, l'appel du vide of joining an unwinnable battle in a destroyed city, the fatalistic welcome for a squadron of enemy fighters that broke off to chase only her, the disdainful roteness in executing a score of aliens downrange.

Were those real feelings, or was Kyouko imputing false emotion onto mere actions? She doubted herself, suddenly.

If they were, these weren't the actions of someone truly trying to protect Humanity. They were the grim battles of someone seeking a fight noble enough to justify their end.

Finally, a different sort of memory began.

---

On the edges of yet another battlezone, Homura silently tailed an alien ship.

She had followed the Goddess's instructions here, and as always the results were fruitful: this frigate‐sized ship was not only a different design than any other she had seen, it was behaving very strangely. Far away from any friendly ships, this ship's normally reliable alien stealth was flickering off and on at erratic intervals, causing the ship to appear to jump around on her sensors. Its course was evasive and inconsistent, but the general direction—toward the barely inhabitable fifth planet of the system—seemed unmistakable.

A heavily damaged ship, then?

They want to be seen, but not in any way that allows a target lock, and pull observers toward that planet, Homura thought, seemingly to herself. That's not a theory I would have ever come up with. I'll have to take your word on that.

A second of silence.

I'm really going to have to take your word on that, Homura thought.

Another pause.

You know I don't doubt you on the details.

There was no apparent target for Homura's thoughts, and while it was reasonable to think her caught within the delusions of a deeply corrupted soul gem, Kyouko thought otherwise. Homura had always had a special relationship with the Goddess, and her own twin of the Ribbon.

Still, it was something to witness Homura speaking to Her on closer terms than probably anyone ever. Kyouko almost felt jealous.

In the memory Homura sighed.

You say this is going to be important, but it's not going to be important enough, is it? Not anytime soon?

Her voice was strained, and Kyouko didn't like the intonation on 'enough'.

Never the straight answer. I'm glad it's that important, at least.

Homura fell silent then, and the memory focused on the ship she was following, which appeared to be entering low orbit of Agni Five, which had yet to receive a proper name, though it did have a pair of automated groundside monitoring stations.

Then, with an urgent alert, Homura's ship warned her about a series of projectile launches towards the groundside stations, something she was little equipped to deal with, not if she wanted to stay back and out of sight. And was it really worth saving some monitoring stations?

For that matter, why were the aliens even bothering to target these?

The alien ship began to leave orbit and vanished back into stealth, even as more sensor information arrived about the projectiles: not missiles, not standard impacters, more like drop pods than anything. Infantry? But a bit small, and clearly angled at the monitoring stations.

Homura considered the matter, then dove her ship in after. By all standards, she was being astonishingly reckless; the volume of active sensor scans, and now an atmospheric entry, would have taxed even the best of the MSY's stealth mages to hide.

---

It seemed Homura was unconcerned about being detected by an alien warship, and nowhere in the memory was it clear why.

The memory recording was palpably incomplete, clear sections of mental state and motivation omitted from the record. However Misa had received this memory—the metadata tagged it as one she had received much later—Homura hadn't wanted to share too freely. Still, the intrigue had clearly perked Homura up, and there was more energy in her motions.

It would have been difficult, likely impossible for even the best ship to catch up to the set of descending drop pods, and Kyouko wasn't surprised to see Homura's trajectory shallow out, as Homura stood up to don an orbital jumpsuit.

Only a magical girl with the right powerset might have reached the ground intact in time to see what was going on, and while Homura wasn't known to have the right powerset—well, Kyouko was willing to bet any one of the Mitakihara Four could have pulled it off, one way or another.

The memory skipped forward, and now Homura was already in the air approaching the ground. It didn't escape Kyouko that the missing time might have been someone—Homura or Misa—concealing the exact nature of the power used.

At the moment, though, she had somehow passed the drop pods on their way to the ground and was slowing herself down rather conventionally with telekinesis, the only wrinkle being that she seemed to be inside a magic stealth bubble of some kind.

The drop pods themselves had proven to be neither explosive nor packed with alien infantry. Instead, a fly‐by sensor scan had suggested they were filled with electronics of some kind. Homura would have snatched them straight out of the air—if it weren't for the unknown magic signatures she also sensed nearby.

---

Rather than reaching the ground itself, she pulled up, unfurling a pair of wings to soar a few hundred feet in the air and cast her eye over the scene, magic senses keen for anyone approaching her, even as she flew an evasive pattern, just in case.

At the moment, at least, Homura's wings looked white and angelic, not the twisting black abominations of New Athens.

But the magic signatures were veering towards the drop pods instead. It wasn't impossible for this planet to have magical girls stationed defensively on site, just surprising—again, there was nothing here worth the protection.

But as Homura's eyes honed in on the signals, she saw something that caused her to take pause, pulling into a vertical hover to stare. She had still yet to spot any actual people, just a triplet of flying drones, each corresponding to one of the magic signatures. They were too small to have a person inside, right?

As she watched, the drones moved into position below the drop pods, as if they fully expected to survive the impact. But surely—

A pulse of magic, and then the drop pods began to slow. Like the signatures, that pulse had come from the drones.

Homura blinked in surprise. For a moment she weighed the possibility of getting closer to get a better look, or even take another scan of the pods, but decided neither was likely to get her more in the way of information. If she wanted to know more, she would have to be more direct.

She swung over a bit closer, making sure her position would not be so close it was immediately threatening, but not so far they couldn't get a good look at her.

Then she reached out, attempting a two‐way telepathic handshake with all of the drones. It didn't work, which somehow surprised her.

"Hello there!" she transmitted instead, using a standard Governance frequency.

As she waved, feeling just a touch silly, she checked her corners for any sign of a magic or technological trap. She wouldn't have done this at all if she didn't think she could take them in a fight, push come to shove, but Ancients didn't get to be Ancient by being careless.

The drones visibly jolted in reaction, much as a human would, and one of them began to circle.

"You are Akemi Homura, or wearing an imitation of her body," one of them thought, mental voice young and female as she would have expected of a magical girl. "With similar wings and powers."

The girl was doing a decent job of shielding her emotions, but Homura could still detect a layer of nervousness underneath. Natural enough, she supposed.

"I am she," Homura thought. "Though I admit having no direct way to prove it at the moment, if you don't recognize my magic. But who are you? And what's with the bodies?"

Now two of the drones were circling.

"A contrivance to provide us concealment and freedom of operation," the previous drone thought. "But why are you here? We knew you were likely alive; indeed we have instructions to speak with you if you ever appeared."

Not the most elegant of conversation openings, and the drone had dodged her real question, giving only the answer that was guessable.

"I followed the erratically‐behaving alien vessel that dropped those canisters," Homura thought. "Allow me to get to the point. You three appear to be three magical girls contained inside artificial bodies, collecting canisters from a strange alien ship. This aroused my curiosity, and I took the risk of appearing here and asking you who you are and what you're doing. And now, I suppose, I should ask you what you mean when you say someone gave you instructions."

That was the gauntlet laid down, but Homura had found in the past that it was often best for everyone to just get things said rather than beat around the bush.

"Shall we land?" the drone asked. "I can explain a bit as we fly."

The drones flew toward the ground, and Homura followed cautiously, staying a careful distance away.

"This is probably self‐evident, but we represent a group that operates on the fringes of Governance. It is no secret that Governance seeks to direct the future of Humanity along its own lines, and to keep its grip on all Human populations. Perhaps the intentions are noble, but we believe this leads to unnecessary human suffering, and the inhibition of human potential. There must be better ways. Better utopias than Governance has constructed."

Homura was immediately, instinctively wary. The message was ideological, and Homura had met many such ideologues in her time. Those who tried to operate outside the system could be very dangerous, even if their intentions were good.

Of course, she had been such an ideologue, once. Twice, if you counted her lesser role in the formation of Governance itself.

Still, what she heard didn't necessarily sound good. There were reasons why the MSY had insisted on spanning all Humanity, and why Governance had aimed for a single, united utopia.

They reached the ground seconds later, touching down into the coarse red and brown regolith that dominated the landscape here. Somewhere, far away, an ocean of plankton kept the atmosphere oxygenated, but most of the land was still uncolonized.

Homura kicked some of the rocks aside.

"Is that an idea you three came up with? Or something you were told?" she asked. "I have heard many people claim to reach for utopia in my life. Governance is the closest I have ever seen, built upon the ruins of most of the others. You'll forgive me if I start off skeptical."

Suffice to say, Homura wasn't signing onto any new utopian projects, rogue colony or otherwise, but that didn't mean she wasn't ready to let them keep talking. They could even work together on the alien pods—if they were relatively harmless and worth working with.

Though any group packing magical girls into mechanical drones was a certain level of dangerous, no matter what. It implied the presence of a capable soul mage, a willingness to dabble in research directions marked forbidden by the MSY, and the time and resources to actually complete the project. They couldn't be taken lightly.

"A reasonable mindset," the drone thought. "What Governance offers is certainly the safest option, given limited information. The thing is, we don't have limited information. We have complete and accurate predictions of the future, within reasonable bounds. Enough to be certain about what we say."

Homura's hackles rose immediately.

"I have it on good authority that precognitive magical girls went extinct centuries ago, and that they're not coming back," she thought. "And I believe my sources more than I believe you."

"No, no," the drone thought, tilting slightly in consternation. "Definitely not precognition. We are aware of that metaphysical limitation. This is purely a predictive engine, a Laplace's Demon transforming whatever physical and magical data we can acquire into projections of the future. Thanks to magic, we can overcome certain information theoretic limits and predict the outcomes of our actions with a precision normally reserved for physics. Albeit, we don't know why magic allows such precision—this seems like a metaphysical loophole that wouldn't be allowed. We'd be interested in your analysis, though that's a conversation for later."

It was often to your benefit to rattle someone in a conversation, so that they might leak information to you. So it had proven again here, accidentally. And while Homura had no intention of sharing such things, the answer was probably that whatever 'engine' they were using wasn't perfect enough for the Goddess to have screened out of the timeline as too corrosive to Human potential. It helped to have a little insider information on the matter.

---

Kyouko couldn't help but raise her eyebrow at that tidbit of information. She and the Church had always suspected as much, but here was Homura thinking it, presumably with direct information. She was sending this one straight to the Theological Council.

---

"I see," Homura thought simply. "Back to the main point—and you think this engine will let you build a better utopia than Governance?"

"Most certainly. Though really, we're thinking multiple utopias rather than just one. It's a core point. Rather than hashing it out here, in these awkward circumstances, we'd be happy to invite you to meet our leading members elsewhere, now that we're done with our business on this planet. Our ship can lead you. They could explain things much more clearly than I can."

That was certainly an offer, and one Homura was inclined to take, with the proper precautions. There was a simple point for her to challenge, though.

"Before I agree to that, about this engine you refer to: I assume it only works on a macro‐scale? After all, you seemed surprised by my presence here."

There was a brief, meaningful pause.

"Well, truth be told, we are sensitive to variables that we don't fully understand or which defy prediction," the drone replied, with a clear undertone of embarrassment. "The honest answer is that you are one of the most prominent of those. That's the reason why we've been told to be on the lookout for you specifically. We'd hardly need to be on the lookout if we knew where you were. But to be clear, we are usually confident in our micro as well as macro predictions."

Well, that was a pretty clear question to ask the Goddess about when she had a chance. But for now, she could defer most of her questions for later. Yet something else about the situation bothered her.

"What about your companions here?" Homura asked. "They haven't said anything. Heck, I don't even know your name. Though I'd understand if you'd rather not share."

It was often natural for only the leader of a group to speak, but Homura had been growing quietly suspicious: something was subtly off about the magic aura of the other drones. Of course, it could be credibly said that it was a consequence of being inside a small drone, but it didn't sit right with her. She had been in the company of those who had been heavily mentally‐edited before, and this felt just a little like that.

"Oh, you noticed that?" the drone replied. "The truth is, a bit of light Reformatting is necessary to fit inside these drone bodies and prevent soul rejection. I've undergone it myself."

The other drones perked up and sent their greetings, but neither that nor the suspiciously convenient explanation sat well with Homura.

Though if they were that upfront about it, she had to admit she didn't have much more to go on than that feeling, but—and Clarisse loved talking about this—for an Ancient the feeling was often more important than anything.

She would go anyway—the offer to just take her to the group's leaders was too tempting to reject. Still, she would keep her guard up—she hardly knew how to do otherwise. Even when she wanted to throw caution to the wind and gamble with her life, she always ended up hedging and making backup plans. It was second nature, and her past experience meant she understood much too well the many ways a single scenario could go wrong.

Even with her powers, she could still get lured into and trapped within a remote star system. She was confident in her ability to extricate herself out of most situations, but interstellar travel without a ship still eluded her, and she had already lost one of her ships to an FTL missile a month prior. She had another one stored, but still.

Despite that, Homura honestly hoped these magical girls were as dangerous as she felt they were, perhaps even more so. Protecting the world a little longer was the promise she had made the Goddess, and all she had done recently felt like puttering around, making small differences here and there. Had the Goddess finally led her to a worthy task? One that might absolve that which bound her to this world?

She set that thought aside and focused on the matter at hand.

"If you are willing to take me to your leadership, then I will go, provided I receive some assurances about my security," she thought. "But I see no reason not to discuss a little first—"

She stopped there, startled despite herself by an urgent message by tightbeam from her ship. She had instructed her ship to contact her only in case of something really important, but her annoyance faded when she learned what had happened.

She resisted the impulse to look up at the sky or show an additional reaction, and found that the drones clearly knew what was happening too, surprise clearly written in their movements.

Another alien ship had appeared out of stealth and fired on the alien vessel she had been tracking, destroying it utterly. It was now on its way to the planet.

---

Kyouko echoed Homura's sense of shock, and paused the memory to try to understand it in retrospect. They had known about the existence of multiple alien factions—Kyouko considered visions from the Goddess absolute in this regard. Internecine conflicts between two alien ships were thus entirely possible.

---

Homura's shock faded too after a moment, though more from emotional self‐control than anything. She watched the drones in front of her; it was obvious they were concerned about the new ship. How they had noticed the alien attack was no great mystery, she supposed—presumably they had their own ships or other scanners she hadn't detected. They hadn't detected her either, after all.

Homura sent no instructions to her ship, which she had to trust to do the smart thing and hide itself as much as possible.

The drones skittered erratically in circles for long seconds, before huddling together in what was obviously a conference of some kind. Homura resisted the urge to telepathically break into one of the follower drones' minds—she was no mind‐reading expert, and while most magical girls wouldn't notice her intrusion, the operative word was 'most'. She would have to content herself with passive telepathic observation.

"You should hide yourself," the lead drone thought to her directly, finally. "The aliens are certainly capable of recognizing individual humans when they bother to try, and you are a particularly notorious individual. I can't predict how they'd react. Best not to find out."

Homura was starting to grow increasingly skeptical of these drones' supposed 'predictions', given the fact that they had now been surprised twice, first by her, and now by this alien ship.

More importantly, the discussion clearly implied the aliens were here to contact the drones, which raised so many questions it was hard to keep count. But the right thing to do now seemed to be to do as suggested and hide. If they betrayed her to the aliens—well, she could win that fight.

She had already reengaged her personal stealth, and could only hope the aliens hadn't already scanned the area. Lifting off, she chose an outcropping a kilometer or so away that would give her a vantage point on the drones. Staying in the air gave her better vision, but staying close to the ground was just safer and more concealed.

Some minutes later, the bloom of distant fire in the sky signaled the entry of the alien vessel into the atmosphere.

Homura dialed her soul gem down even further, maintaining only the bubble of stealth she was using to hide, and kept her head down, figuratively as well as literally.

The alien ship eventually swooped into the air nearby, buffering its descent with antigrav even as it blasted dust and rocks across the landscape. The drones stayed impassive, a pulse of blue magic appearing to shield their delicate mechanisms from the debris.

The frigate dropped into place with a quiet thud, the dust blowing off the surface refusing to stick to the metamaterial hull, which shone pristine.

Homura found herself holding her breath. Despite everything, the moment got to her: it changed the face of the whole war, if the aliens were talking to any humans, even those hostile to Governance. It meant she could potentially get in there, and even run interference.

The side of the alien ship opened a few moments later, flexing slightly as a circular door slid open. With no delay, an alien in an armored exoskeleton stepped out into the air, falling to the ground with a ponderous thud. Its movements were eerie, but all too familiar to Homura at this point.

What was different was the appearance of the suit, which had ornamental gold‐and‐dark‐green stripes. She hadn't seen that before. It was difficult not to speculate that this alien was more senior.

Homura was trying to plot in her head how she could possibly eavesdrop on what was going on. No human had previously communicated with the aliens successfully, but unless they were going to start arranging rocks into the prime number sequence it was obvious they had to have something, and if that something involved short range laser transmissions Homura didn't really have an option but to get right back in there and record what she could, an onerous proposition.

---

Kyouko frowned at that thought from Homura. How exactly was Homura expecting to go stand right in the middle of several magical girls and expect to be undetected? Clearly, Homura had previously‐unknown stealth capabilities, but it was one thing to have developed a bit of a side power, like her own fire powers, and quite another to have mastered it so completely.

Fortunately—or perhaps unfortunately for Kyouko's hopes of a power demonstration—it didn't come to that.

Instead, one of the drones produced an orb‐like object from a compartment that opened on its side, and though the baseline design looked visibly alien, it was clearly an enchanted device.

Kyouko recognized it instantly. The same or very similar object had been seen in the recording they recovered from the asteroid, used to hold the false negotiations between Governance AIs and Cephalopods.

Homura naturally couldn't recognize it, and was thus still trying to puzzle out the nature of the magic when the orb started speaking.

---

"As discussed previously, artifacts and communications from other Thinker factions are to be handed over to us immediately without inspection. We are here to collect."

Homura contained her surprise and had time to ask herself:

Thinker? Is that what they call themselves?

One of the drones replied audibly over speakers, in a sharp female voice.

"Of course. But we must protest the abrupt nature of your intervention. We had the situation under control, as you see."

The orb pulsed, briefly changing from its original light‐blue to sharp red.

"Past experience has made it quite clear that the temptation of knowledge represented by these artifacts outweighs your commitments to us. We are here to remind you that we are watching."

The drone replied:

"We have protested before about your refusal to let us know basic facts of importance to us. Partners must operate under a spirit of basic cooperation."

They don't seem on happy terms, but partners? Homura thought. Other alien factions? My opinion of anyone who works together with the aliens is quite low, but if there is more than one alien faction, then perhaps there are some who can be negotiated with. Perhaps even these can be.

Homura was once again addressing the unseen Goddess, and seemed to receive an answer this time.

Alright we'll discuss plans afterward, she thought. Clearest answer you've given me yet. I suppose you brought me here to show me this, but couldn't this have happened earlier?

A short pause.

Naturally.

Homura turned her attention back to the alien conversation. The alien was now rebuking the drones:

"Partners are expected to stick to the terms of agreements reached, not litigate details via subterfuge. This topic was discussed at length previously. If Utopia Unbound wishes to reopen the topic for negotiation, your leadership should do so formally. For now, we will take the canisters."

More useful information. The organizational name didn't tell her much that she hadn't been told already, but this proved that the aliens had extensive dealings with them, and moreover understood them as a social construct. It had not been clear, prior to today, that the aliens were capable of understanding humanity much at all.

The drones moved forward with what Kyouko imagined was reluctance, opening side compartments to disgorge their canisters, leaving them on the ground. A set of small drones scurried out of the back of the alien's suit, picking up the canisters with small metal tentacles.

"We will be in touch," the alien said through the orb, with what Homura swore was a brusque tone, followed with some kind of tentacle gesture.

Homura watched as the whole sequence of events reversed, the alien jumping back into its ship, the ship lifting off—again buffeting the area with an oppressive cloud of dust and regolith—as the drones stayed silently in place.

Then, once the ship was a distant speck in the sky, it vanished, in a flash of radiation that seared her eyes with the intensity of a magnesium flare even from a couple dozen kilometers away.

There had been no missiles or attacking ship this time—Homura's ship confirmed it. Had those drop pods been bombs after all? No, the radiation strongly implied an FTL engine overloading—perhaps the pods triggered it?

Homura signaled to the drones that she wanted to speak again and quickly flew back over.

"Self‐destruction," the drones informed her immediately. "The pods were harmless, I think—the aliens always do that. They're worried about mind‐control."

"That seems incredibly extreme," Homura said, with unfeigned shock.

"It's their policy," the drones said. "They're not concerned about these individual messengers."

Nor did the drones seem overly concerned with the fact that they had just revealed an apparent alliance with the enemy. Homura simply couldn't let that slide, even if it jeopardized her chances of meeting with their leadership.

"Care to explain yourselves, then? I don't have a high opinion of Human factions cavorting with genocidal aliens."

She moved cautiously and slowly—if necessary, she would fight it out. This was no longer simply a matter of investigating a rogue group of magical girls.

"They discovered and captured a few of us before the war even broke out," the drone thought. "The aliens were and are overwhelmingly powerful, more even than you know. We were able to make an arrangement that guaranteed our survival. We admit that what happened at New Athens defied our expectations. We anticipated a short war. The vast majority of humans were to be spared."

As before, this drone clearly had no idea what she was dealing with, or how to speak to an Ancient in general. The gaps in that explanation were wide enough to drive a fuel tanker through, and it took Homura no time at all to come up with a list of cutting questions. For instance, that clearly implied they had expected New Athens to go down as a loss for Humanity, possibly taking much of the MSY with it. And it was obvious that whatever 'arrangement' they had made would leave their conspiracy on top.

She focused on the core point of outrage, though.

"I don't know what kind of arrangement involves carrying out genocide on innocent planets," Homura thought. "If what you say is true, that happened after you talked with them. Without involving the actual Human government, mind you."

"Their soldiers don't see killing the same way we do," the drone thought, with palpable discomfort, "and their leadership is not interested in opening negotiations with Governance, not until they can safely dictate terms. And the aliens remain confident in the inevitability of their final victory over Humanity."

"Then you've failed to explain to them the nature of magic," Homura thought. "Even what you know ought to be dissuasive enough. Did I not kill enough of them at New Athens? Little of what you say makes any sense."

She was barely holding her tongue, but by now she had chosen to play along. It was obvious they were an enemy, but if she was careful and pretended to be talked down, perhaps she could learn something more.

Or they would try to kill her, now that she knew they were complicit in genocide. They had made no move toward attacking her yet, but that didn't mean much; perhaps they simply predicted that attacking here would be futile.

"I haven't told any lie," the drone thought. "Believe me, we didn't want those massacres, nor do we want aliens to dominate Humanity, nor are we fighting by the aliens' side. Unfortunately, that doesn't matter. A long war is acceptable to them, and they prefer certainty in their long‐term security over sparing human lives."

For the first time in this conversation, Homura sensed a clear lie through their mental defenses. Not that the drones had been particularly honest before this, but it had all felt like misdirection and technical truths, nothing she couldn't have detected just from the words. But this time her passive telepathic sense provided an extra crumb of information: while they didn't enjoy the slaughter of Aurora and Atlas, they did see those crimes as useful to their cause.

Most likely, they had predicted the invasion would lure out most of the MSY's fighting strength at New Athens—right into the sights of an orbital superweapon.

Homura made sure to show no sign she detected the slip. She couldn't ask too many questions, or it'd be obvious she was milking them for information. But her guise allowed her a few more questions, she hoped.

The most important question first:

"And what about this talk of other alien factions?" she asked. "As far as anyone else knows, there is only one alien faction. There seems to be some tension between you and the aliens just now about those factions, and whatever they sent in those canisters."

"At this point it's probably best if we just take you to our leadership, as we previously discussed," the drone thought. "Any explanation we could give here would be incomplete, and frankly I don't necessarily know all the details."

…and I don't know what I'm allowed to say, and it might sound bad. That was another clear telepathic read. So much for the questioning.

Homura pretended to think about it for a moment, while actually taking the time to think about personal security arrangements.

"Alright," she thought finally. "Please, let's both call our ships in, and I'll follow you in mine. I hope you'll understand if I want to travel by myself, and have eyes on you."

"I have to admit that makes sense," the drone thought. "I'll call it."

At her direction, Homura's ship broke radio silence, informing her that a new blip had appeared on sensors, lifting off a few hundred kilometers away for the short hop over to their current location. The appearance of the ship on sensors had caused certain anomalies that strongly resembled an alien ship decloaking.

Her own ship began its descent at the same time. There was no telling who would have the advantage if either ship opened fire: neither side had an appraisal of the other's capabilities, even if Homura's had the energy advantage of being at altitude.

But there was no incident, and when the drones scurried onto their ship—of a Human make and model at least—Homura boarded her own, the two ships taking off simultaneously while bombarding each other with an array of active scans.

The trip to orbit, then into intrasystem space, gave Homura some time to collect her thoughts and ask a few questions.

How big a danger are these people? Am I to focus on them, rather than the aliens and the war?

The distinctive pause.

Finally. This feels like real progress. I just hope it will be quick—perhaps within the year?—and I don't have to kill too many people.

Another pause.

I admit that's not what I wanted to hear.

Even with modern starships, trips into interstellar space were hardly fast. She asked for a destination, and was sent the coordinates of an uncharted system a dozen light‐years away. Unfortunately that was still most of a day.

Long years of practice had made Homura skilled at maintaining a kind of passive situational awareness, and even as both ships cruised along, maintaining light stealth, she placed herself in a kind of meditative state, magic suppressing the need for sleep. Suitable for days or weeks of loneliness.

So when an alien cruiser dropped out of stealth three‐point‐seven hours later, accompanied by a pair of FTL missiles nearly on top of her, she was able to react in time.

---

Again there was a very poorly placed timeskip, and now it was obvious Homura's memory was holding something close to its chest. Something about what exact magic Homura was performing. Kyouko would have found the situation Homura was in quite a pickle, and she didn't know Homura to have any kind of teleportation magic, and yet the next scene was on board the ship of the drone magical girls.

Correction: Homura hadn't originally had any kind of teleportation magic, but she had used something similar three times the last time Kyouko had seen her, right after New Athens. So, perhaps it wasn't so strange.

---

Homura stared at where the soul gems had been in her palm. She had tried her best to capture the drone magical girls alive, but somehow the soul gems had burned themselves out, minutes after she had taken them, despite her best attempts to apply stasis.

Some kind of soul magic she was unfamiliar with, most likely. Well, the Goddess would show more mercy to them than she would.

Homura stepped over the shattered drone bodies and passed her magic over the pilot's command console. A civilian transport normally had nothing in the way of internal defenses, and it seemed her opponents had not added any while making modifications. Nor was there a full onboard AI, and the relatively light security meant that it took remarkably little effort for Homura to commandeer the controls. She was hardly an electronics expert, but she had been forced to pick up a trick or two over the years.

There would be time to screen the ship for tracking devices once she got away. For now, the important fact was that the ship's alien stealth device was still active, ironically hiding her just as well from the alien cruiser as the drones had probably intended to hide from her. Her own ship had been destroyed, she had lost her captives, and the drones had reduced their translation device to ashes, but on the whole, she still felt victorious. Finally, a goal was within sight.

There was no time to waste. She wouldn't make the same mistakes twice. She had work.

---

From there the memory transitioned back to a montage of fleeting moments, with just enough detail to make the timeframe clear, obviously intended more to provide context than elucidate anything of depth. Some of it was presumably simple summarization.

Homura tried, initially, to find and extinguish this conspiracy herself, stubbornly ignoring the Goddess's clear suggestions to recruit some help. This took her well outside the usual Human circles, away from the battlefields and into the obscure parts of Human space, tracing every rogue colony known to both Governance and the MSY.

Then she explored outside Human space, using the human‐operable alien stealth device she had obtained from the drones' starship to penetrate deep into the Sonoran sector. She found some alien supply lines, and work being done on what Kyouko recognized as something similar to the wormhole station destroyed in the Saharan Raid, but no alien home worlds or TCF conspiracy—Utopia Unbound—home bases.

Her only substantive finds after months were a pair of seemingly‐abandoned conspiracy listening posts—similar to that found by the Task Force, Kyouko thought. A substantive hint, but not enough.

Meanwhile, the war situation went from bad to worse. Sure, some of the initial attacks had been turned away, but every time Homura returned, more systems had fallen, with losses now concentrated in the Indus Sector. All this despite the largest mobilization that Humanity had ever seen.

More than once Homura had wondered aloud whether the Goddess was sure the war was not already lost and more than once she received an answer indicating… that it was at least not the worst case. On a few occasions Homura intervened when in the area, saving some colonial militia ships, and even personally stopping an attempt to bomb a shipyard. But she knew it was pinpricks relative to the scale of the war, and when she intervened, it was more of a personal gesture, to make herself feel better.

At points Homura seemed to consider recruiting a follower, someone to work with her, as the Goddess was clearly implying was necessary, but she never quite followed through. Her options were limited anyway: a newly‐minted magical girl from a rogue colony would hardly be terribly reliable, and this didn't seem the time to pull anyone away from front‐line combat. Nor was Homura interested in making contact with anyone from her past life.

Then the narrative reached a point that got Kyouko's clear attention: Homura pulling into orbit of New Athens on the anniversary of the day she had saved the planet. On that day, down on the surface, Kyouko had given the most important speech of her life.

---

This hardly seems like a fertile place to find useful agents, Homura thought, addressing the void.

Okay yes, there are a lot of magical girls here, but what, do you want me to walk up to one of them and just talk to them? No, don't answer that, of course you do, but I'm not going to risk revealing myself so close to Kyouko of all people—yes, same planet is plenty close, in my opinion. Why do you think anyone would even believe me? Obviously I'm just a crazy Ancient talking to a ribbon in my hair.

There was a long pause.

You spoke to Kyouko? I thought you were always against revealing yourself to more people. Just to give me a base of recruitment?

I've always admired the versatility of your acts.

There was another pause, and then Homura sighed.

You really think they'll listen?

---

Kyouko couldn't help but feel a shiver, unrelated to the cold of Yenisei.

It was one thing to accept intellectually that your life, and your recent upending of it, had been part of the plan of a greater power. It was another to see parts of your plan baldly sketched out, in a manner that didn't seem to leave much room for your agency.

She had indeed had her own talk with the Goddess. The Goddess had never told her in plain terms to found the Church, or even to recruit followers. She had actually gotten the impression the Goddess was very reluctant on the matter. Kyouko had offered her ideas, arguing that magical girls needed, more than ever, the hope that Homura's secret could provide. So many girls were being thrown into relentless, bereaving combat—it was like the old days, before the MSY. Even if no one believed her, she had to at least try to offer them comfort.

The Goddess had never even explicitly agreed, implying only that She wouldn't try to stop her. Kyouko had even felt guilty about ignoring Her apparent wishes.

That was the understanding with which she had poured out her heart at New Athens. Knowing the Goddess a bit better after a couple decades, it did not surprise her to learn that She held more than one perspective on the matter, and that there was some degree to which her choices weren't her own. But emotionally, she couldn't help but feel manipulated.

That was a sensation she hadn't felt in a long time. Even Homura and Yuma had usually avoided leaving her in the lurch.

A disturbing realization then crawled over her: this was surely how Ryouko complained about feeling in the reports. How Maki felt, about Kyouko's interventions in her life.

A thought she had to file away for consideration later, probably with a lot more food on hand. For now she had to swallow her feelings and press onward.

---

I should have known you had something like this up your sleeve, Homura thought, once the speech was over and there had been time to look at the local net's reaction. Of course, a few minutes was far too short to really know if the fire would spread, but she could easily read the winds.

Really, she should have known Kyouko had it in her. That was a real blind spot—after so many centuries, she had never really expected any of them to feel Her again in this life, even with one of Her ribbons. But it made sense, because the Goddess tended to only kick pebbles when She intervened. Rarely ever boulders.

Well, to be more precise, she was the boulder. At least when Clarisse van Rossum wasn't serving the role.

But whatever success Kyouko might have soon, Homura was still reluctant to make direct use of it. Sure, she could see the value in a recruiting pool that was conditioned to take her word on the Goddess and the nature of her mission, but that solved only one of a succession of problems.

She took a few seconds to mull that over, and then her ship notified her of an incoming transmission.

To say that was unexpected was an understatement. Homura knew from experience that the alien stealth device she was using was very, very good, and should have kept her hidden in orbit from all but magical clairvoyants, none of whom should have had any reason to look for her up here.

There was only one possible chink in her armor: to listen to the broadcast she had been obliged to request a tightbeam signal, which was an obvious risk, except that Homura could easily perform the minor bit of magical hacking necessary to spoof a legitimate request. She had even spent the past few months refining her techniques.

Not enough, apparently.

The message was itself by tightbeam, originating from a way station on the surface. The authentication claimed it was from someone she knew: Jeannette Smith, on behalf of her wife Yasuhiro Rin.

Homura sighed. Of course. She knew she'd been too sentimental, coming back here.

For a moment she considered simply fleeing, but abandoned the thought—if Rin and Jeannette wanted to expose her, they could have done so already. Her best chance of preventing that was to simply talk them out of it. In fact, that was all the message requested: a chat.

As for how that damned couple knew it was Akemi Homura they were addressing—well, being infuriatingly perceptive was Rin's special talent.

She sighed and dictated a response: she would meet with them, if they agreed to travel to a particular location in deep space, where Homura wouldn't be observed decloaking.

---

It turned out, Rin and Jeannette contacting her was a blessing in disguise. They had repeated Rin's Unification Wars disappearance trick, picking up new identities and lives to look for a worthy cause, and eagerly signed on to work with her. And frankly, Homura couldn't have picked better candidates than a magical girl detective and an electronics specialist.

It had worked so well, that is, that it carried the clear whiff of higher planning. 'Blessing' indeed.

Homura had never been averse to looking even a divine horse in the mouth, but this time, after an indecent amount of nagging on her part, she received an unanswerable reply: the expansion of the newly‐established Church of Hope had another hidden purpose, one which mirrored a purpose Homura's own little conspiracy would have. The 'Laplace's Demon' that the enemy had mentioned was a serious threat, and the Goddess intended that Her two ribbons would cover its eyes. She did not like exerting influence upon Humanity, but Her divine intervention was necessary to bind the Demon's power. Given that tension, She preferred having as many pebbles as possible to nudge.

That, and one or three boulders, of course.

---

To say that this revelation would be explosive within the Church was putting it rather mildly. The Church knew quite well that the Goddess had mixed feelings about its existence, but why they were allowed to worship Her now had always been controversial. The common answer, promoted by Kyouko herself, was that they were necessary to support magical girl morale and war mobilization, that they were a beacon of hope in the darkness. Homura's version was… much less inspirational.

Like so much here, Kyouko had to put that into a mental box to think about later.

---

When Homura relayed that information to Rin, it brought a new revelation.

Rin and Jeannette hadn't abandoned the flailing war effort just to fulfill some wanderlust—they had, even prior to the war, begun to grow suspicious of something slightly wobbly in the ever‐turning wheels of Governance, some kind of ineffable magical influence that lay at the center of several anomalies she had tried to track. That the war suddenly forced the MSY to enter Governance's fold made them even more suspicious. But after nearly a year of effort, they had failed to derive all but the faintest leads, which had only made Rin more certain—nothing eluded her that long without deep magical support.

Her original reason for signing on with Homura so quickly had been to check if it was her—apparently her third most likely theory. But their brief time together had made clear that wasn't the case. Rather, Homura's information about 'Laplace's Demon', and experience with magical girl drones, explained much. Some kind of magical predictive engine could dodge even Rin's machinations, if it were powerful enough, and if it acted via agents whose existence violated old assumptions.

Homura would have liked to be smug about outmaneuvering the legendary Yasuhiro Rin, except she knew damn well the Goddess had been leading her by the nose. Moreover, she didn't like the way Rin was now openly making a project of untangling the Goddess's historical influence on everything that had ever happened.

But she liked even less the conclusions Rin began reaching now that she was in the fold. First, that they had to keep recruiting; unfortunately, Homura was now outvoted three to one on the question. But second, as they added new members, Jeannette finally completed the pattern she and Rin had been working on the last year: the conspiracy Homura had been trying to find was also responsible for a breach in the TCF.

For a while, plumbing the depths of the breach, and what it was being used for, was their highest priority. Their little cabal—which Inoue Yoko eventually dubbed the Coordinating Group—spread itself thin across the stars, tracing the evidence with growing horror. Governance, the MSY, the Armed Forces—all were fatally compromised, with Laplace's Demon directing a surgical program of magical patching and unpatching that evaded all magical audits that might reveal it.

Yet so much was inexplicable—not just the age of the digital backdoor, which they traced back to shortly after the Unification Wars, but rather, the mildness of the exploitation. Utopia Unbound appeared to only be cloaking their operations and gathering data!

It was Rin who pointed out, though, that even a breach of this scale couldn't be exploited in unlimited fashion, precisely because of the need to constantly dodge magical audits—fatally compromise the war effort, yes; execute a bloodless coup, no.

So, apparently, the drones hadn't been lying about the limits to their cooperation with the aliens. But that was little comfort. And now the question was: what to do about it?

---

That exact question dominated the debates of their Coordinating Group. The natural answer was to try to coordinate with Governance and the MSY and seal the TCF backdoor all at once; unfortunately, Jeannette's projections indicated that there weren't enough magical girls with the right powers, nor fast enough technological methods, to do it in time. Even a couple hours was more than enough for Utopia Unbound to cripple the war effort.

There was a second obvious answer: execute a decapitation strike.

Some groundwork would be needed: first, they needed to actually find Utopia Unbound's leaders, and then they needed a technological solution to block IIC communications, so no command to exploit the TCF breach could go out. No such technology existed yet, but with time they could perhaps induce Governance to develop something for them.

This approach was advocated for by several members, and had the appeal of being both complete and seemingly straightforward—something that Homura had long ago learned the value of. After all, as Napoleon had said, when setting out to take Vienna, take Vienna.

Unfortunately the checklist of things that could go wrong was simply too long: the leadership might not all be in one place, there might be a dead man's switch, and they had to not see it coming, even with Laplace's Demon.

If Utopia Unbound were ever truly endangered, and they realized it, they could sign on fully with the Cephalopods, wringing whatever leverage they could out of the incredible mounds of intel they held, not to mention the Human shipyards and fleets and exotic matter refineries they could sabotage. With the current state of the war, and frankly, in any probable near future state, that was tantamount to offering the aliens victory.

Utopia Unbound might not be traitors to that degree yet, but if cornered… well, they had already sold out Humanity once.

That put Homura's Coordinating Group in a frankly depressing bind, and they spent some weeks thinking through how they might escape.

One unpalatable approach was to attempt negotiations with Utopia Unbound. Homura felt that her past encounter with them was more than enough evidence of bad faith in that regard, and besides, no one wanted to contemplate what kinds of concessions might be demanded. Jeannette called it 'surrendering without a fight' and Homura couldn't really disagree.

Another suggestion was a form of strategic stalling: wait for a moment in the war where Humanity had enough of a temporary advantage that it would be safe to patch the TCF and undergo the risk of Utopia Unbound sabotage. Better, but hardly easy to calculate or achieve, especially anytime soon.

The nature of the war troubled them, too. Governance simulation and standard logic made one conclusion clear: any aggressive alien power ought to be overwhelmingly powerful, enough to overrun Humanity with barely a fight. The statistically likely differences in civilizational size and age made it almost a guarantee. Even magic shouldn't have been enough to bridge the gap, barring heavy divine intervention. That Humanity had held out already for over a year was incredibly implausible a priori.

Nonetheless, the explanation for Humanity's continued independence had to lie within that implausible space, and the most obvious explanation was that the aliens were not fully invested into the war. That was even consistent with what the Utopia Unbound drones had told Homura, and the apparent internal conflict among the aliens.

But, frankly, that assumption wasn't useful on its own. A careless attempt at negotiation with the various alien factions could easily backfire—it certainly didn't seem like Utopia Unbound was pleased with the results of their negotiations. Though that didn't mean they couldn't try.

For now, only one clear path presented itself: to lead their enemies into a deep, twilit forest, and then strangle them there. It had to be over before they saw it coming. To accomplish that against a currently superior foe, whose strength lay in predicting the future…

Someone had done that once—alone, even—but Yuma had faced opponents with much more serious restraints, and a precognitive who might very well have let her win. Lacking such advantages, their counterplot would have to be so exquisitely precise, yet so devilishly insidious, that even Laplace's Demon could never anticipate it.

Fortunately, that was possible. Unfortunately, Homura knew exactly from Whom they might obtain such a plot.

---

Homura squinted at the sheet of metal in her hands, laser‐etched to atomic precision with row after row of inscrutable petroglyphs, each a pattern of four symbols arranged within a circle. It might have been mistaken for a lost ancient language, but there was something about the curves involved, the connections between the quarters, that suggested something ineffably alien.

Or so she liked to imagine. The atomic precision was, of course, pointless, since she had designed the etchings entirely from memory, based on an image the Goddess had cast into her mind. It was, She claimed, a message in an alien language, one that would help convince a friendly alien faction of her goodwill.

Only help. The friendly aliens' previous five attempts to make independent contact with Humanity had been sabotaged by hostile activity, either from compromised Governance AIs, Utopia Unbound agents, or false flag attacks from the attacker faction. They were on the verge of giving up, and after repeated hostile receptions, they weren't likely to believe her claims on their face.

The question then was obvious. Why was she being given a single document to hand over instead of, say, a translation guide to the alien written language, or even better, a way to get an enchanted translation device like Utopia Unbound had? At the least, she could take an enormous box of grief cubes and sojourn with the friendly aliens, spend however long it took to build up a common language, even hash things out via hand signals if she had to.

Patience, she had been told. The document was efficient, limiting the extent of Her meddling. Full mutual understanding, enough to enchant a translation device or properly communicate, required a certain sacrifice. Moreover, and more importantly, limiting contact with these aliens for now would produce a better final outcome—a proper diplomatic exchange too early would lead to dire consequences, barring extreme interventions on Her part.

Would this be like the Unification Wars? Homura had asked. Would She mostly let this war play out, too, acting only to help prevent the worst possible outcomes?

That question had caused only sullen silence. She didn't like discussing the topic.

The Goddess had never wanted to stand athwart history. Never mind that her power was limited, she had no right to dictate people's choices in life—Her succor came only at death. Nonetheless, her good nature led her to often steal from mortals the worst possibilities, and she felt fewer scruples about adjusting Humanity's course as a whole. She framed it as guiding everyone toward their own, better impulses. She tried not to interfere in anyone's clear, reasoned choices.

But, even knowing that, Homura and her Goddess hadn't spoken much, in the latter years of the Unification Wars. They had both felt guilty, and not without good reason. Yet in those days, Homura had at least been able to take solace in the thought that with a United Front victory, the establishment of a lasting peace, and the founding of Governance, her earthly duties would at last be fulfilled, and she could finally rest.

She had been wrong. And then, at New Athens, wrong again. How much hope could she have left?

Homura hated to think it, hated to consider the notion, but she felt sure that the Goddess could have respected her wishes, could have asked less of her, could have shared more with her. How come the Goddess could accept Miki Sayaka's wish, but not hers?

Sometimes, Homura felt that Sayaka must be laughing at her, up there in the timeless aether.

Not that she thought the Goddess was lying about the big picture, about whatever stopped her from just giving the friendly aliens, Homura, and Humanity what they thought they wanted. Oh no, on that, they were aligned. She was well aware that sometimes it was necessary to take some losses in the short‐term to improve the long‐term. Perhaps even serious losses. That the Goddess didn't like talking about it just showed she still cared.

No, it was ultimately about Homura's own, selfish desires. She had a closer relationship to the universe's only divine being than anyone, and still she wanted more. The Goddess was opening up to more magical girls now—couldn't Homura have more, now, too? More magical girls were giving their lives in defense of Humanity than ever before—couldn't Homura, too?

And all she had gotten was the same responses, over and over. She supposed when you were timeless there was never really an occasion to compose a better response.

Well, for now her only option was to play along. The aliens couldn't be easily communicated with normally, thanks to an incompatible telepathic interface and alien mindset. The block of hieroglyphs in her hand was all she had to work with, unless the Goddess chose to give her more.

Even setting up this meeting had required retrocausal information, which taxed the Goddess's resources. Homura had piloted a ship in personally to receive the transmission—a rudimentary encoding of the local star map with location circled—and echo it back, intended as an affirmation. According to her special source, this would prevent the same transmission being picked up by a Governance deep space probe and subsequently diverted by Utopia Unbound.

And now she was here, orbiting around a silent world roaming the interstellar void just inside the boundary of the Nile Sector. Without divine guidance she would have been very nervous about her position, alone and plainly uncloaked in a civilian‐class ship that could be blown up at a whim.

At least she had gotten very used to this kind of travel, filled as it was with lonely views of a dark horizon far from any of her kind. Or even the Incubators, for that matter—she was hiding from them, too. She had learned the technique from an ex‐SMC soul mage some centuries prior, before she died on mission in Pakistan. It was one of a few cards she had kept close to her chest all this time, withheld until she needed it most.

She almost jumped when the sensors registered an unknown ship inbound to the system at FTL speeds. This happened more than she liked to admit: her mind, sitting on idle, letting too much time slip away.

It only took a few more seconds for her ship to process the finer details of the sensor profile and lack of human transponder signal and conclude that, yes, this had a 98% chance of being an alien vessel. No attempt was being made at any kind of stealthy approach—if anything, they were trying to be seen.

All of which boded well, of course, even if she felt a tinge of nervousness about the possibility of such a ship triggering one of Governance's deep space border nets. Surely they were remote enough here?

She had to take entirely too much on faith nowadays.

At this range, it would still be dozens of minutes before they would arrive at the planet, so Homura sent a signal in the clear: a ping with no informational content, meant only to be acknowledged.

The reply came back almost immediately, disregarding travel time: a repeat of the ping with the same characteristics, clearly not a natural reflection.

It was difficult not to be impatient as the minutes passed, and Homura found herself fiddling with her hair, knowing full well that the aliens didn't care a single whit what her hair looked like. Like Kyouko, she had never allowed Governance hair implants on her scalp. Hair care was simply part of her centuries‐old routine, and she hadn't wanted to lose it.

She remembered… no, it was better not to think about that right now.

At length the alien ship grew near, and it began to fire a repeated infrared beam at a location on the planet's surface. Combined with the trajectory, the meaning was clear: they intended to land, and intended her to follow.

She had anticipated this. Docking procedures in space were hard enough without needing to deal with alien locking clamps and airlocks, and potential hostility and ambushes. Dropping to the surface made them both a bit more vulnerable as well, but it didn't bother her much: she certainly had no intention of attacking her alien guests, and she knew there was no way the Goddess would let her drop into danger here.

Well, perhaps a little danger, but never any real risk.

She was becoming a little too grumpy with the Goddess, she chided herself. Here, at least, she was doing something quite real. And it wasn't like the planet's surface was a vacation destination—without the light of a star, the only question about most rogue planet surfaces was what flavor of frozen gas or rock you would be standing on, and how many dozens of Kelvin the ambient temperature would be, which affected how long your environmental suit would last.

Really, trying to coordinate a meet‐up there was only moderately easier than it had been in space. That the aliens had chosen a place like this showed what their mindset was like after the previous disasters.

She had come prepared for this possibility, of course, as well as the possibility of needing to attempt a docking, or make a spacewalk. Thus, she was already wearing the right underlayers and could step right into the necessary ultra‐low temperature environmental suit.

As the ship lowered itself toward the surface—specifically, a wide stretch of shallow ice plains only a few centimeters deep—she picked up her message‐engraved plate, vacuum‐sealed into a protective sleeve. If necessary, she had prepared backups, and could even shine the message through a special filter on her flashlight.

It took only a few seconds for the ship's thrusters to sublimate the ice below, and then she stepped out onto the bare rock. A surface was a surface, no matter how frozen.

Homura pulled out a pair of magically‐enhanced farsight goggles she had cribbed from the MSY, a pair that dated back to, of all people, Mikuni Oriko.

It turned out she had hardly needed to bother. The Cephalopods were already waiting, a pair of them standing in plain view a hundred meters away in their own suits, both of them large and barrel‐shaped, far larger than Homura, or indeed any of the numerous alien combat troops she had killed in her time.

That alone was strange. She had seen on the battlefield that the aliens had a diversity of combat or computing augments, but this was on a whole different level.

Still, sensor scans showed they carried no apparent weaponry, though the very nature of the environmental suits meant that they leaked very little informative radiation.

One of the aliens moved aside as she approached, lifting one of several arms to gesture at a glowing panel on the side of their ship. The message was obvious: they wanted her to board.

It was a big ask, in a way, since aboard the alien ship was hardly neutral ground, but Homura could hardly blame them after their previous encounters with humans. And as before, she herself had little to fear.

She hoped the Goddess's implied protection wasn't making her too reckless.

She had prepared as well as she could, but it was still an understatement to say she had no idea what to expect. She had dictated all kinds of contingency plans for various outré scenarios to her cortical implants, fully expecting that she would have to play everything by ear regardless.

As someone had said once, plans were useless but planning was everything.

She jumped up towards the alien ship, barely catching herself on the side of the door when it slid open just a bit too slow. Right. She was showing a bit too much power.

She felt a tad naked taking off her environmental suit in the forcefield airlock, all too aware that even with her magic, being ejected back into the near‐vacuum outside would be unpleasant and annoying, especially were she slow to get a bubble up.

Then she raised an eyebrow when she stepped inside the alien ship proper, making a special note in her memory logs to review everything she saw later. It was simply different from the alien ships she had seen before, in ways both subtle and not, supporting the Goddess's claim that they represented a different alien faction. In particular, there were a number of strange thin metal rods embedded throughout the room—sensors of some kind, presumably.

Overall, though, she was a bit relieved to see that she was looking at a scenario three: in front of her was an obvious conference table, complete with two trios of seats facing each other, with the seats on one side obviously more suited for humans.

For now, though, the room was empty.

She pulled a scanner out of her pocket and waved it over the room, checking it with her magic at the same time. Hopefully the aliens wouldn't mind a little due diligence, as long as she carried it out as visibly as possible.

That was when the oversized door at the far side of the room irised open, admitting another Cephalopod that was as grossly oversized as the ones outside. Without the suit, her scanners could read more clearly what was going on—as best as her sensors could tell, this alien had a prodigious amount of implants in its core, enough to require a dedicated heat radiator in the back. But it didn't look like weaponry—if anything, it looked like computing. They really had mastered biotechnology, it seemed.

The alien sat into one of the comically oversized seats on the other side of the table, bending down with a grace that she wouldn't have given them credit for. Then it gestured with a large arm‐tentacle toward one of the human chairs. The message was obvious.

Homura couldn't help but look over the chair one last time—it rather resembled a piece of custom‐molded plastic—before taking her seat. It shifted to her presence, like many of the modern human chairs, but was just a little off, poking her in one of her lumbar vertebrae.

As she did, the door to the airlock once again slid open, and the two aliens that had been outside stepped in single‐file. Part of Homura wanted to remain on edge, tense against the possibility that sitting her down had been a trap to render her less mobile. She had to actively calm herself, and realized, with an almost perverse sense of relief, that the Goddess's protections had indeed not dulled her sense of danger.

The other two aliens took their seats, making clear that Humanity was a bit underrepresented here relative to their expectations. Homura wondered if she should wait: the aliens probably had some attempted communication scheme cooked up.

She decided to take the initiative. The Goddess's pictogram message should be self‐explanatory, and would skip a lot of potentially unnecessary throat‐clearing about who had what motives.

She pulled the metal slab out of the sleeve on the side of her garment, holding it up for a moment for everyone to look at, before setting it on the table, where it was bombarded by the inevitable barrage of sensor scans, one of the aliens leaning ponderously over.

Once that activity had calmed down, she reached her hand out and pushed it forward, though by now the aliens should have spotted the quite clear inscriptions—and judging by the tentacle gestures, they had, or so she imagined.

The one in the middle picked it up immediately, human‐like eyes casting over the surface.

The reaction after that was almost comical, the three aliens squeezing together to peer at the piece of metal barely wider than one of their arm tentacles. She doubted they lacked the human ability to simply take a picture of the slab and sit back into their chairs to study it in their heads, but they preferred to study it in front of them. Very human, in a way.

At brief intervals they exchanged glances, and the occasional twitching arm wave showed what was going through their minds. With a reaction like this, there was no doubt that they understood the slab, as the Goddess had promised.

Not that she had ever doubted.

She knew what it said, of course, approximately. It explained that Humanity was not willfully resisting the demands of the aliens—that, in fact, the main human government had never received any set of demands, only a seemingly‐unprovoked, genocidal attack. It explained that magic‐empowered bad actors had sabotaged their previous attempts at communication, and would continue to block future attempts as well. In the document, Homura promised that her faction would work to defeat the problem, but that she needed time—lots of time.

That was not the most inflammatory content in the document. That would be the section discussing the faction of aliens attacking Humanity, which was also magically compromised by some of the same bad actors as were afflicting Humanity, and who were the real blockers on any diplomatic contact. The aliens Homura was speaking to would be erased in a 'combat accident' if they tried anything direct, and it was imperative they return home immediately to report their contact before anything else happened to them, via the very particular route and schedule provided. The other faction already knew they were in the area.

It was difficult to expect any communication of such complexity to be conveyed by one message, no matter how well‐written, but Homura had the advantage of divine providence. The Goddess claimed that most of the answers to any questions they might have were already embedded, which perhaps explained why the aliens were still reading, and why the glyphs had to be so small and dense.

But some things would still require another interaction. The document promised the aliens clear proof of Homura's ability to predict the future, apparently involving fine measurements of the behavior of a certain pulsar, and that would take time to resolve. Moreover, they were supposed to provide her with certain schematics and pieces of technology to reverse‐engineer, and presumably couldn't whip that out of a hat. There was an arranged drop‐off before the aliens left Human space—in exchange, the Goddess told Homura, she was to provide an enchanted container protecting a specific number of empty grief cubes.

Homura didn't know most of the details, not yet, but she supposed things would soon be clear enough.

After some conference, one of the aliens pulled an electronic tablet from a fold in their robes and slid it in front of her. The message was drawn in pictures rather than text, a picture of her face with an arrow pointing to another star map location, this time in what appeared to be deep space. They had agreed.

Above her head in the picture was a set of inscrutable symbols, but she could guess the meaning. It was the name she had given herself, written in the style of an alien culture, a name that the aliens probably didn't understand and that the Goddess had disapproved of: Akemi‐Homura⊃Divine‐seeking.

---

The plan the Goddess had sketched out to her after she retrieved the friendly aliens' gifted technological package was elaborate and time‐consuming, in a way that sparked serious concerns among those she was working with. She did her best to assuage them, but in her heart she shared many of the same thoughts, and more besides.

She had known defeating Utopia Unbound would take some time and technical effort, yes, and she had been prepared to be at the task for years. But even an optimistic assessment of the Goddess's plan estimated roughly thirteen years. Could the war truly last into the 2450s?

It was difficult to imagine that a Goddess with knowledge of the future couldn't achieve better, even with self‐imposed constraints on restricting free will, unless there were other long‐term considerations at play.

It wasn't the human she had once known, to sit on a celestial throne weighing billions on a scale, and they both knew it.

---

Here there was another gap in the memory record. Subtle enough to miss, but Kyouko noticed. Whatever emotions Homura had felt here were simply missing, faded to a simple thought exposition. Kyouko could hazard a guess as to why.

Moreover, it was a glimpse of the kind of person the Goddess had once been.

---

Sadly, she had learned that lesson back in the Unification Wars. Now, for this new Contact War, Homura felt sure they were in the same kind of situation, and Homura did not like it. Was this why the Goddess was keeping her in the dark? To preserve her sensibilities? Homura was not as loyal to the Goddess's divinity as to Her humanity, and this flew in the face of that.

Would she simply accept that again? Before, she had thought to return to her Goddess's side, and save her that way. Now, she worried the Goddess had no intention of letting that happen.

If she were younger, and thereby more foolish, Homura might have considered…

---

And here the memory skipped again.

---

Still, she put on a brave face, resolving to diligently execute Her plans as Her Human part would. She and Rin and the rest of the group plotted out a plan for containing Utopia Unbound without alarming them unduly—ideally, without even letting them know anything was amiss at first. Despite the need for secrecy and mobility, that required more resources—personnel and grief cubes far in excess of what they currently had, to spread their tentacles far and wide. That meant recruiting at scale, as subtly as possible. It also meant scrounging and stealing materiel, ships, and even financial assets in less‐monitored colonial markets.

Sensible.

Also sensible: as a matter of due diligence they made continued efforts to contact members of the friendly alien faction. Even if they couldn't properly communicate, they could perhaps gain more alien technology, or at least make it clear they hadn't just taken their technology and run—although, unfortunately, Homura suspected it would be a long time before they would ever have the chance to prove otherwise.

They had also, after some debate, experimented with trying to communicate with the more unfriendly aliens, which at least were easily found. Despite some rather creative attempts by both Jeannette and Sophia, they were completely unsuccessful, just as Governance had been since the war began. Several cornered aliens committed suicide. Mind‐reads, as much as they could be understood, indicated that all the aliens they could find had been mentally stripped‐down. Even having Homura herself sit deep within alien territory and broadcast in the clear, hoping to contact alien leadership, had no result—to her frustration, she wasn't even attacked.

But the Goddess had other, more controversial directives.

The alternate TCF lines could at least be chalked up to divine prescience. As a human and erstwhile citizen of Governance, Homura was instinctively quite concerned about the ramifications of making an alternate TCF, whatever the security reasons. It would have warranted at least a little thought. But in this case, she had no reasons to doubt the Goddess when She said it was a good idea, and necessary, and that was that. She suspected, given the war, she could probably maneuver Governance into undertaking that effort for them.

But there was another project, one that bothered Homura much more.
