The key lay in the technology package that they had requested from the friendly aliens at the Goddess's behest. Purely on a technical level, it was clearly the most important technology package ever received, a set of artifacts, data crystals, and engraved diagrams detailing or demonstrating a variety of biotechnologies outside standard human reach.

Or at least they were supposed to be. The outlines of it all looked promising enough, but the contents were essentially unintelligible on their face, and clearly the kind of thing that required a dedicated research team and an unknown number of years, something they very much did not have.

The only reason they knew what was in there at all was the Goddess's explanation of what she had asked for and what to do with it. And this was what gave Homura the most pause: somewhere in there was what both the aliens and the Goddess considered the most important, some kind of mental communication organ, one that would align human cognition with alien well enough to enable telepathy.

According to the Goddess, figuring out how to build and grow the thing would be one of their most important tasks—and it needed to be grown from birth. Implanting one in an adult was possible, but much more difficult, and there were drawbacks for magical girls in particular.

Homura didn't like any of the implications of that, much less the practical: she and Rin simply hadn't built their organization around any kind of scientific nucleus. Instead, they had focused on investigators, spies, and agents. Inoue Yoko, Sophia Aaronson—skilled operatives yes, biologists no, and they were already out combing for others of their own kind. It simply seemed like the best way to do things, even if the Goddess had implied the thinking there was too short‐term, and that Homura should stop being so stubborn.

In the end, as always, the Goddess got Her way. The long‐term approach had to be investigated, even if it pulled them down a path they didn't like.

So they started looking for biologists, technicians, researchers.

---

"Smuggling technology of this magnitude into the Governance research programs would be quite a feat. They'll be bound to know something is up if it just appears from an unknown institute."

"Not to mention we don't quite understand enough about it ourselves. There would need to be a whole project around it. With our limited resources, we've made very little progress. Ideally we could tap Governance resources to do the research for us."

"Can we recruit a prominent researcher? Someone already in position for something like this?"

"Would take a lot of doing, but maybe. Would have to make sure we can trust them."

"I have a better idea."

Homura stood up, peering down at the others at the conference table. There was a diversity of eyes staring back at her, polite, beseeching, skeptical. Nearly all were magical girls, but there were two human scientists mixed in, one of them even male—both rescued at the last second from marauding aliens and brought on as scientific advisors.

Represented here was about half of those she had managed to recruit to her fledgling organization, pulled in by personal charisma, loyalty to the Goddess, or detailed argumentation. Those missing were on assignment elsewhere, and the strain was tremendous—even with some ability to tap into Governance resources, it was proving nearly impossible to coordinate with numerous agents across interstellar distance while still maintaining coherent planning.

"I am confident in my own ability to infiltrate as a researcher, provided we generate an adequate amount of cover," Homura said, "but of course so far I have been forced to spend all my time here. However, our rivals have shown us the solution: simply be in multiple places at once. Or so we've recently discovered."

She paused to let the astonished murmur flow around the table.

"You want us to split our souls like they do?" Pratiwi Surija asked. "We're still not sure that's safe. Nor are we sure how they do it. Nor—"

"No, not like we think they do," Homura said. "Not even if we were desperate. There are some lines not to cross lightly. But I do have some ideas, and I am willing to be the first test case myself. More importantly, I've asked, and it's safe and should be possible. There can be no better source."

There was an uneasy silence. While the vast majority of those present were willing to accept the word of Homura's Goddess, it still wasn't unanimous, and it was a test of Homura's credibility every time she invoked Her. Still, her occasional uncannily accurate predictions of the future went a long way.

"As long as this experiment doesn't risk you personally," one of the others said. "You're too important. Maybe one of us should do it."

Homura prided herself on her legendary impassivity, so she really hoped that her tinge of annoyance didn't show. It was a reasonable sentiment. She shouldn't lay her personal issues onto them.

"If I think I'm in any danger I'll consider it," she lied.

---

The years passed, just as Homura had feared, while in the background the war continued to expand—the aliens had invaded the Rhine Sector, and then the Mekong. Fully one‐third of Human sectors were now being invaded; morale in Human space was low. Many feared alien ships would soon see Sol itself.

Homura and the Coordinating Group knew better, but it wasn't much comfort.

Her organization broadened the scope of their recruiting, discovering on the way that the dark corners of Governance space hid a lot more than they imagined, with both unknown rogue colonies and quite a few magical girls, and others, in seclusion.

Some of those put Homura and the others in a moral quandary, caught between their need for personnel and a cast of candidates that ranged all the way from soul criminals to the merely very untrustworthy. Some they recruited anyway, others were best to just leave alone, and still others required immediate elimination.

At least there were a few rogue colonies Homura could take personal satisfaction in having leaked back to Governance—though of course it would be some time before Governance could focus on them. She tried not to think about the ones they couldn't find, but knew existed, like the fraudulent colony mission that had eluded her early on at San Giuseppe.

Meanwhile, Homura acquired the scientists and technicians she needed, some using her new connections as 'Joanne Valentin', and quickly discovered their utility.

Firstly, there was the practical matter of developing technology and techniques to subsist in secrecy, modifying Governance implants to allow them to pass. They even picked up one or two AIs along the way, rigorously magically screened—it was strangely gratifying to have them accede to their mission, once it was sufficiently explained and proven, and useful to have someone capable of making the necessary modifications with the certainty of AI.

But secondly, and most interesting, perhaps, was the original reason they were here in the first place, the data package they had received from the friendly aliens.

They had finally begun to make progress decoding and reverse‐engineering the contents, even if the whole topic threatened to boil Homura's mind over with frustration. It seemed almost unfair to think this way, to ask a divine entity to provide technology—but surely the Goddess could furnish a translation guide, at least?

But, there was still progress. If nothing else, some of the biological techniques provided had helped them build the body of Joanne Valentin, a mundane clone of a volunteer without a trace of direct magic. Of course they knew how to clone, but many of the finer points of modifying the brain to be closer to Homura's required the mediation of neural implants with plenty of alien technique.

Though in truth, the main body of innovation was still magic‐based. The neural implants made the process easier, but they still needed her soul gem to perform the main body of work. After that came the really hairy part, involving deeply experimental soul mage techniques to 'dilute' her soul into the new body. The very concept was worrisome, even to her, but it was so useful she had even done it more than once, since it allowed her to keep many irons in the fire.

Routine regroupings allowed her to synchronize herself across copies, and with time they had expanded the process to others. Only the original body with the soul gem could use magic—unlike Utopia Unbound—but they were working on a process for at least transferring the soul gem to another body, so she could use her magic to infiltrate without looking like, well, Akemi Homura.

This kind of expanded scope, along with their improved roster of field agents, allowed them to more regularly catch sight of Utopia Unbound's operatives—even if that had resulted in several skirmishes, and a couple fights to the death.

Despite their better preparation, it seemed the drones still couldn't be captured alive, but they could at least extract some tangible intelligence to pry open more of the enemy's operations. What they had found so far was suggestive, in a disturbing kind of way.

Utopia Unbound seemed obsessed with information gathering, with a constellation of long‐range monitoring stations and even a handful nestled in remote regions of Governance worlds. Given how Laplace's Demon was described, it made sense.

But beyond that, Rin's tracking of rogue, TCF‐breach‐induced logistics shipments suggested the existence of sites engaged in clandestine research. Hardly too alarming on its own—Homura's group was itself doing the same—it became so once one considered what Homura had heard of Utopia Unbound's aspirations. What kind of a utopia required so many secret research facilities?

They had to know what the group was up to. The manifests alone suggested research into magic, and alien technology, an alarming combination even in the best circumstances. But attacking the facilities was for now out of the question; for now, they needed to avoid any significant escalation.

Moreover, their handful of successful mind‐reads had indicated that many of the drones they were fighting were heavily Reformatted, and not even responsible for their actions. But that moral angle couldn't hold them back, not with these kinds of stakes. If necessary, they would apologize in the afterlife.

Finally, for the Coordinating Group's peak project, the alien communication organ…

Truthfully, she was nervous about that. They were only barely ready.

They had a while ago worked out the main details of the mental communication organ whose design the aliens had sent them—though it seemed to involve much more than communication, now. The original data had described alien cell types and neurotransmitters, but thankfully the principles of biological pattern‐matching still applied. Function could match even when form did not. The aliens had also been assiduous about laying out some key abstractions for consideration, though it had taken her brightest minds a year to understand what the diagrams were even intended to represent.

There was much they still didn't understand of its functioning, and Valentin née Homura had to admit certain reservations about implanting a design about which they knew so little into a human fetus.

But in the end, neither she nor the rest of their leadership had wanted to wait any longer. The whole process had taken too long already, and of course, just as she was preparing to find or engineer a candidate mother, the Goddess Herself presented a candidate, one that worked in her own lab.

All too convenient, in a taxing and wearisome kind of way. Valentin had quite liked Kuroi Nakase, had even attended her wedding. Why couldn't She just reveal these things from the start?

---

There was a brief lull in the montage there, a slow moment among what was otherwise a jarring barrage of mental exposition.

---

Valentin sat in her office, sipping impatiently at a cup of coffee, trying not to think too hard about the procedure under way just a few doors over.

It made no sense for her to perform the procedure herself. Plainly, she didn't have the skills. But the waiting and the lack of direct involvement ate at her.

She looked at the ribbon she had hidden in her pocket and touched it with one hand. The gesture brought her little serenity.

She sipped more coffee.

---

After that, there was only the painful wait, made better by the fact that at least the war was finally stabilizing. Hardly won, or safe, but the aliens had clearly overstretched themselves, bypassing too many worlds and leaving their long supply lines exposed. Much of the Rhine had been retaken, and the deepest incursions into the Indus, Mekong, and even Ganges had been cut off. The aliens still had the strategic initiative and were clearly plotting something, alongside ever‐persistent raids, but it gave them all some breathing room to work with.

It was also nice to see that Humanity was producing plenty of technical innovation even without Valentin‐injected gifts—Von Rohr's forcefield work, for instance, which had nothing to do with anything Homura was involved in. Moreover, Homura felt confident that Valentin was now deep enough in Governance's scientific establishment that she could begin directly introducing technology.

In particular, she was interested in establishing a brand‐new generation of TacComps as a biotechnology‐based solution surreptitiously based on a new TCF branch—a direct contribution to the war effort that also protected against TCF corruption. The sooner she got moving, the better: even now, she estimated it would be at least a year or two before such a project could get off the ground.

In the meantime, their shadow conflict with Utopia Unbound had entered a phase of what might be called strategic mutual avoidance. They watched each other carefully, almost incessantly, but took immense pains to avoid being detected. That didn't mean a lack of violence—attempting to eliminate each other's watchers was a routine solution to the 'problem' of being spotted, and even ship‐to‐ship combat in the orbit of rogue planets had happened on occasion. But at the end of the day they still wanted to avoid an escalation that, even if they won, might drive Utopia Unbound into helping the alien invaders.

As for the other direction… Utopia Unbound actually tried, once, attacking one of their facilities with nearly two dozen drone magical girls and supporting equipment. Unfortunately for them, Homura had been there, and they had been annihilated in ambush.

Since then, they simply hadn't tried again.

There had been some worry that Utopia Unbound would expose Homura's agents to the MSY, but mind‐reading during that attack had revealed that the drones had instructions not to expose the Coordinating Group. Their leadership apparently feared escalation as well.

Instead, while both sides kept away from each other's core facilities, interference activities in the field only got more intense.

They had traced some of Utopia Unbound's own recruiting, both within and without Governance, and attacked this recruiting where they could. Homura's group did all it could to identify every rogue colony being recruited from, and then eliminate the recruitment, either by prompting Governance to quash the colony or by recruiting accessible candidates themselves.

They had also observed the occasional kidnapping on contested or besieged worlds, and subtly interfered, sometimes by just triggering Governance's alien intrusion alarms, then staying in the area to prevent easy use of the TCF breach.

There was also the question of grief cubes.

Their own grief cube logistics they had solved a while ago, as a matter of necessity. While in the past they had managed to secure stocks by tasking every field agent with a dual assignment of gathering surplus when on Human worlds, particularly on rogue colonies, this had simply stopped being practicable after a certain point. So, for all that they found it to be distasteful, they were obliged to start tapping into the MSY's supply, concealing their tracks behind them.

They had plenty of ideas on how to do that, of course, because they had been tracking Utopia Unbound's own efforts in the same direction, which were far less restrained and at times seemed actively malicious. As always, they made efforts to interfere when possible.

All in all, they could accurately assert that they were extending their tendrils everywhere around Utopia Unbound's operations.

Yet they didn't seem to be making an impact, not in any way that showed up in the level of their enemy's activities.

Partly, it was just hard to tell. Their penetration of Utopia Unbound was awful—Laplace's Demon made for an excellent watchdog—meaning that neither side had any direct insight into the other.

But it still seemed very likely they were missing something, and it was Rin who first suggested that Utopia Unbound was recruiting—or coercing—people cornered by the aliens on conquered worlds. That kind of thing would be very difficult to verify in the field, and would be invisible to Governance if executed correctly.

Nor could they do very much about it, yet.

They had other initiatives. One very useful thing, prophesied by the Goddess, was that their very presence interfered heavily with Utopia Unbound activity, simply by confounding their predictions.

But too much of that would let Utopia Unbound trace their interference, and so they realized there was a simple trick: help expand the Church of Hope. It had much of the same effect and couldn't be blamed on anyone in particular, except perhaps Kyouko. Utopia Unbound would hopefully write it off as some incredible inconvenience brought on by the Ribbon.

That did mean that they spent a surprising amount of effort influencing Governance policy and subtly protecting Kyouko and the Church, when they could do so unobserved. This was a necessary task: Governance was innately hostile toward religion, and it was doubly wary of a fast‐growing 'cult' reducing its already tenuous authority over magical girls.

Valentin herself subtly encouraged her colleagues, including a couple AIs, to investigate the Church's effect on the war effort. Their concrete positive results served as a powerful institutional armor for the Church.

---

The memories cut out there, both Homura's and Misa's, leaving Kyouko with far too much to digest at all at once.

Misa spoke immediately, not yet giving her a chance to recover.

"Like I said, most of that I learned much later—some memories about the Goddess Homura only shared in the last month. But on New California, we did learn about how the Trusted Computing Framework had been compromised, and about Utopia Unbound, and the aliens. Stacy and I both agreed to have our memories erased; I offered to work for Homura some time in the future, if she needed me. Hermina—well, she was already officially dead, so they couldn't just set her loose. She joined up. Survived until I joined too, thank the Goddess."

"Okay, you can't just blast me with all of that at once," Kyouko thought, struggling to organize her thoughts in a way that she hadn't experienced in many years, not counting Maki. She needed time to think.

Kyouko handed over the data crystal reader to Van Rossum. Impatient, Gracia got Van Rossum to agree to let her mind‐read alongside her—they sat down together in the Tanaka posture.

Kyouko did find some amusement watching the looks on their faces as they absorbed the memories. What a day.

After a few minutes, they finally stood up.

"I don't even know where to start," Gracia thought. "What are we even supposed to focus on?"

"Yeah, imagine how I felt," Misa thought. "On New California, she wouldn't even tell me what poor kid she had installed this creepy alien biotech project into. I think you've figured out who that is, though."

Kyouko had, of course. She knew her own mentee.

Oh Goddess, that was another can of worms. She hoped Shizuki Ryouko could forgive Homura. And the Goddess.

"Okay, I have many questions," Van Rossum interjected. "Let me see if I have this narrative straight. The Goddess set Homura against the TCF conspiracy back in 2440, right before she fell off Internal Security's radar. In 2441, the Goddess arranged a meeting between Homura and the 'friendly aliens' that we saw attempting to negotiate with Governance in the video from the asteroid. They gave Homura the biotechnology to build whatever alien brain organ they use to communicate with each other, and Homura's scientists then figured out how to build that into Shizuki Ryouko, so that, over a decade later, Ryouko could go successfully negotiate with the friendly aliens. The Goddess insisted it had to be Ryouko, and it had to wait until that much later, in order to prevent worse possible futures. In the meantime, Homura's conspiracy infiltrated themselves into Governance using cloned mundane bodies, and was fighting a cold war of some kind against the TCF conspiracy as late as 2445, the last memory. But clearly that continued escalating, because by 2450 in New California she was regularly going out to destroy Utopia Unbound's facilities herself."

Kyouko was newly impressed by Van Rossum, and barely avoided staring. How had she kept track of all that?

"Pretty much," Misa said. "But while I'm giving you all this quite valuable intel, there's a question you haven't asked yet, though you've probably thought of it. If I'm willing to show you all this, why couldn't Akemi Homura come herself?"

"Surely she could have at least used one of her extra bodies, if she was worried about capture," Van Rossum commented.

The man Misa was wearing as a body smiled oddly, shrugging and looking off to the side in a way that was just a tiny bit uncanny, or so Kyouko imagined.

"Can you imagine? She wanted me to convince you to just trust us that we're doing good, with only the barest details. She knew better than that on New California, and I know better than that now. So instead I'm telling you a lot. I would say it's a bit of a rebellion inside the group, but really it isn't—it's most of us, trying to operate outside the strange lines Homura has drawn."

"So what do you want us to do?" Gracia asked, aghast. "You're telling us this like we're supposed to help you. How?"

Kyouko held up a hand to interject.

"If you tell us where she is, even just where one of her bodies is, maybe we can talk with her. Is that the idea?"

"Maybe. We don't know yet. That was all only one piece of what I'm here to tell you. The truth is, there's a bigger problem than Homura refusing to meet with you all: not long after the TCF breach was repaired, Homura started refusing to speak with the Goddess."

She looked between the three of them for their reactions. Gracia looked a bit overwhelmed, Van Rossum looked thoughtful, and Kyouko…

"Why after that?" Kyouko thought, turning it over rapidly in her mind. "No, wait why at all? She has a Ribbon in her personal possession, and a personal relationship. That's a level of direct guidance She gives no one—gave no one, until Homura recently, apparently. We knew she was special, but—"

"I wouldn't go so far," Van Rossum interjected. "Remember, I got quite a few instructions myself, long ago. Maybe not all the time, but the guidance was pretty direct. And I'll admit here that I was and am still not happy with all of it. Though I can't say I really understand Homura's reasons here. I had moral qualms. I don't think that's her problem."

"Well, regardless of how it happened, it's definitely happened," Misa thought. "And none of us have been granted any Ribbon guidance either, not even when Prometheus fell. So we're stuck. We pulled off the Goddess's twenty‐year plan—Shizuki Ryouko is going to set off a chain reaction that will end the war and save Humanity. That was the whole point. But we don't know what the follow‐through is. Are we really supposed to just sit back and watch? Some of us in the Coordinating Group don't think so—hell, Homura doesn't think so. For the first time we're flying blind, and if something doesn't change, I think we're going to crash."

"And Homura still thinks she can't ask us for help," Kyouko thought, putting a hand on her head. "What's wrong with her? We really do need to talk with her."

Misa was silent for a couple of long seconds. Kyouko had found it difficult to read her slightly uncanny body language, but was starting to learn—Misa was uncertain, and nervous, in a way that she was trying to hide.

"It won't be that easy," Misa thought finally. "I sincerely doubt she will speak to any of you, even if I were to sneak you in, even if you managed to get close. She doesn't want to be spoken to. The impression we've gotten is that she's only even still with us reluctantly. More than once, she's talked about handing over control to one of us. We've pleaded with her otherwise, but some of us are starting to seriously consider it."

Kyouko took that in for a moment.

"All the more reason to try," she thought.

"Maybe," Misa thought. "We can consider it. I would have to talk to the others. She might really disappear if you try it."

"If I may speak plainly, what even are you all still up to?" Van Rossum asked. "Is there a reason you can't just come in from the cold, so to speak? Sure, there was the stunt at Adept Blue, but is there a reason you couldn't have just warned us, if you knew the aliens were going to attack us?"

"We didn't know," Misa thought. "We hardly know anything anymore. But, given the leak at Persepolis, we figured it was a priority target and needed defense, especially given its connections to Shizuki Ryouko—after all, her grandfather was targeted on Persepolis, which hardly seems a coincidence. It was only luck that we got to Persepolis first, by the way. We were only there investigating Ceph behavior. That's one of the only things Homura has really pushed to do recently; she claims we must be missing something."

Misa shook her head slightly; Kyouko wasn't sure at what.

"Do you know what technique this Utopia Unbound is using to split between bodies and into drones?" Van Rossum asked. "You shared details of what you do, but it's more relevant to us what they do, so we can prepare countermeasures."

Misa seemed to think about that a moment.

"It might be better if I gave you more of my memories to sample, from after Orpheus, and my recruitment. The answer is already in there, and it will give you answers to your other practical questions too. More importantly, I think it will make clearer what's wrong with Homura."

Kyouko thought about asking more questions anyway, while the previous topics were still hot, but decided to save it. The last thing she wanted to do was change Misa's mind.

---
